newsitem.title: TURKEY: Crowds delay trial in death of Turkish journalist.
newsitem.headline: Crowds delay trial in death of Turkish journalist.

text.p: Authorities on Friday moved the high-profile trial of 48 policemen for the beating death of a Turkish journalist to a nearby sports hall after overcrowding in the courtroom prevented the start of the first hearing.

The judge adjourned the early morning hearing until 1 p.m. (1000 GMT) amid jostling by a crowd of more than 200 observers, journalists and officials in the packed courtroom in the sleepy town of Aydin in southwestern Turkey.
"I cannot even see the lawyers and the witnesses cannot go in and out," the judge complained, shouting to make his voice heard above the din.

The trial of the policemen -- 11 of them charged directly for the fatal beating of reporter Metin Goktepe in January -- had been put off from July and moved from Istanbul for what officials said were security reasons.

Rights activists say this was to try to keep the court proceedings out of the public eye, and lawyers for Goktepe's family have said their first demand would be to have the case returned to Istanbul, where the killing took place in January.

Claims of extrajudicial killings and deaths by torture in Turkish police custody are rife. The Ankara-based Human Rights Association says there were 21 just in August this year. However, it is rare that the perpetrators come before the law.
"In a way this is a unique case because it is a clear case," said Jean Chichizola, of the independent journalists association Reporters sans Frontieres (Reporters without Frontiers).

"Since 1988, 21 journalists have been killed in Turkey. In Metin's case, it was possible to know who killed him and possible to put pressure on the authorities to ensure a trial," he told Reuters outside the courtroom.
Turkey's human rights record has long been under fire from Europe, and almost derailed plans for a customs union deal with the EU that eventually went into effect in January.
Dozens of Goktepe's friends and relatives, including his mother Fadime, came to the trial from Istanbul -- some 800 km (500 miles) to the north of Aydin.
A number of Western observers, including a European parliamentarian, also attended the hearing.
None of the policemen charged were present in court.
